userJob: Turn a set of colours found in the subject into a system a page can be built from
problem: A palette is a list of colours, and a page needs to know which one is the action, which is the focus ring, and which foreground goes on which background. Reaching for role names first produces a primary and a secondary before anyone has looked at the subject.
worksWhen: The colours already exist, taken from the subject’s own materials, and the question is what each is for
avoidWhen: Nothing has been found yet. Naming roles first is how a category palette gets in through the back door.
mechanism: Find the colours in the subject first. Then give each a role from a fixed, small vocabulary: background, foreground, action, onAction, focusRing, border, and the optional ones the page actually has. The vocabulary is fixed so a script can check it; the values are not, because they came from the subject.
risks: A role that points at nothing, so the page has an action colour nobody chose and the browser picks it
Ten roles filled from six colours by repeating one, which is a system on paper and one colour doing four jobs on the page
mobileRules: Roles do not change with width. A layout that needs a different action colour at 375 has two actions, not one.
accessibilityRules: Every foreground role owes a background role it is measured against, and the measurement is per pair, not per colour
focusRing is a required role. A focus ring nobody chose is the browser default, on a ground it was never picked against.
genericnessNote: The role names are the same everywhere and that is the point: they are a checkable vocabulary, not an appearance, and the values still come from the subject. The vocabulary is structural inspiration from ui-ux-pro-max (MIT), credited in THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.md. What is deliberately not taken is its category-to-palette lookup, which gives every business in a trade the same colours.

userJob: Know before building whether the text will be legible on the ground it sits on
problem: Contrast is checked at the end by a scanner on a rendered page, so it measures the pairs that happened to be painted in the states the crawler reached. The pair that fails is usually the one that only appears when a field is invalid or a button has focus, and neither is on screen on a first render.
worksWhen: Always. Every page has at least a body pair, an action pair and a focus pair.
avoidWhen: Never, though a page with one colour on one ground can say so in one pair and move on
mechanism: List the pairs, not the colours: which foreground on which background, in which state, and what floor that pair owes. Measure them before implementation. AA is 4.5 for text, 3 for large text, and 3 for non-text such as focus rings and meaningful borders.
risks: Listing only the rest state, which is the one the scanner would have found anyway
Measuring a translucent background as if it were opaque. A colour at nine per cent has no contrast of its own: it needs the stack behind it, back to front, from something opaque.
mobileRules: The same pairs hold at every width. A pair that only appears at 375 is still a pair and still owes its floor.
accessibilityRules: WCAG 2.2 AA: 4.5:1 body text, 3:1 text at 24px or 18.66px bold, 3:1 for focus indicators and for borders that carry meaning
A disabled control is exempt from the floor and is still owed a way to be understood as disabled that is not colour
genericnessNote: This is a measurement, not an appearance.

userJob: Decide whether this page owes a dark scheme
problem: A dark scheme gets added because pages have them. That doubles the palette, doubles the pairs to measure, and produces a second appearance nobody in the page’s actual use scene ever sees.
worksWhen: The page is genuinely read in the dark: on call at 02:00, in a vehicle, in a control room, or by someone who has set the preference and reads everything that way
avoidWhen: The page is read once, in daylight, next to the thing it is about. Say that, and say it in the contract, rather than shipping an unmeasured second scheme.
mechanism: Answer from the use scene. If dark is owed, it is a second set of pairs with their own measurements, not the same palette inverted: a ground that is a material has no dark equivalent that is still that material, so the dark scheme is a second set of found colours.
risks: Claiming dark and populating nothing, which reads as covered and is worse than not claiming it
Inverting lightness while keeping hue and chroma, which produces muddy mid-tones that fail their pairs
mobileRules: prefers-color-scheme is a system preference and has nothing to do with width. Do not tie one to the other.
accessibilityRules: Every pair is measured again in the dark scheme. A pass in light is not a pass in dark.
Pure white on pure black is a real complaint from readers with astigmatism; the dark ground is a found colour like any other
genericnessNote: Near-black grounds with one acid accent are one of the most reproduced looks there is. A dark scheme reached for by reflex arrives there.
